NEW DELHI, India (CNN) -- President George W. Bush called India's prime minister Thursday to push a proposed nuclear partnership that sparked an unsuccessful no-confidence vote against the Indian leader this week, a White House spokesman said. Prime Minister Manmohan Singh won a confidence vote despite opposition to the nuclear deal. "Both leaders expressed their desire to see the U.S.-India Civil Nuclear issue move forward as expeditiously as possible," Gordon Johndroe said. The phone call took place two days after Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh narrowly survived the no-confidence vote in the lower house of Parliament. The vote was sparked by concerns from the opposition that India was kowtowing to the U.S. The tentative deal was announced in 2006 and signed by Bush and Singh a year ago. Under the agreement, which will need to be approved by the U.S. Congress, India would have access to U.S. nuclear fuel and technology for its civilian nuclear power plants. That would happen even though New Delhi, which tested nuclear weapons in 1974 and 1998, has declined to join international non-proliferation agreements. In return, India has promised that it would not transfer the fuel and equipment to its weapons program, and it would allow the International Atomic Energy Agency to inspect at least 14 of its 22 nuclear plants. The plan would also expand U.S.-Indian cooperation in energy and satellite technology. The plan was approved by India's Cabinet last year, and does not have to be ratified by the parliament. The leaders of India's two communist parties -- which hold about 60 seats in Parliament -- have accused Singh of surrendering India's sovereignty to the United States with the deal. A no-confidence vote would have forced Singh to resign, and required the government to hold early elections unless a new coalition could have been formed. The Congress Party-led coalition has governed India since 2004. Tuesday's 275-256 vote was so crucial to the survival of Singh's government that five members of parliament serving prison sentences were freed to cast votes -- under the watchful eyes of their jailers. Shortly after Singh survived the vote, White House spokeswoman Dana Perino praised the deal as "a good one for everybody." "It's good for India because it would help provide them a source for energy that they need, one that is nonpolluting and one that doesn't emit greenhouse gas emissions," she said. "And we think that we can move forward with this. If their legislature lets it move forward, then we can do the same here and then we'll be able to get this wrapped up."

NEW DELHI, India (CNN) — President George W. Bush telephoned Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh on Thursday to urge progress on a proposed civilian nuclear agreement, a deal that had triggered a failed no-confidence motion against Singh earlier in the week, according to a White House spokesman.

Singh survived the confidence vote despite political resistance to the nuclear pact.

White House spokesman Gordon Johndroe said the two leaders “expressed their desire” to move the U.S.-India civil nuclear initiative ahead as quickly as possible.

The call came two days after Singh narrowly won the no-confidence vote in the lower chamber of India’s Parliament. Opposition parties had pushed the vote over fears that India was yielding too much to the United States.

The preliminary agreement was first unveiled in 2006 and was signed by Bush and Singh a year ago. If approved by the U.S. Congress, the accord would allow India to obtain American nuclear fuel and technology for its civilian nuclear energy facilities.

That access would be granted even though India, which conducted nuclear weapons tests in 1974 and 1998, has not joined international nuclear non-proliferation treaties.

As part of the arrangement, India has pledged not to divert the fuel or technology to its nuclear weapons program. It has also agreed to permit the International Atomic Energy Agency to inspect at least 14 of its 22 nuclear plants.

The proposal would further broaden cooperation between the United States and India in areas such as energy and satellite technology.

India’s Cabinet approved the plan last year, and it does not require ratification by Parliament.

The heads of India’s two communist parties, which together control roughly 60 parliamentary seats, have charged that Singh is compromising India’s sovereignty by entering into the agreement with Washington.

Had Singh lost the no-confidence vote, he would have been compelled to step down. The government would then have had to call early elections unless a different coalition could be assembled.

India has been governed by a Congress Party-led coalition since 2004.

Tuesday’s vote, which Singh won 275-256, was considered so vital to the continuation of his government that five imprisoned members of Parliament were temporarily released so they could vote, while being monitored by prison guards.

After Singh prevailed, White House spokeswoman Dana Perino described the nuclear agreement as “a good one for everybody.”

She said the deal would benefit India by helping provide a needed energy source that is nonpolluting and does not produce greenhouse gas emissions. Perino added that the United States believed the agreement could advance, saying that if India’s legislature allowed it to proceed, Washington could do the same and complete the process.

Communist parties and other opponents accused Prime Minister Singh of compromising Indian sovereignty and aligning the country too closely with U.S. strategic interests. They argued that the deal would limit India’s independence in foreign and nuclear policy. Despite these objections, Singh and his supporters maintained that the partnership was in India’s national interest and would bring long-term benefits to the country’s energy security and international standing.

Singh’s coalition government won the confidence motion in India’s Parliament after a bitter political fight over the U.S.-India nuclear deal, which would allow New Delhi access to U.S. civilian nuclear technology and fuel despite India’s refusal to sign the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

Bush, who has strongly backed the pact, spoke with Singh to praise the outcome and reaffirm U.S. support for moving the agreement forward, according to officials familiar with the call.

The nuclear accord, first announced in 2005, is considered one of the central foreign policy initiatives of the Bush administration’s relationship with India. Supporters say it would strengthen ties between the world’s two largest democracies, expand energy cooperation and help India meet its growing power needs. Critics argue it weakens global nonproliferation rules by giving India benefits normally reserved for countries that accept full international nuclear safeguards.

The deal still faces several hurdles before it can take effect. India must finalize safeguards arrangements with the International Atomic Energy Agency, secure approval from the Nuclear Suppliers Group and then return to the U.S. Congress for final consideration.

Singh has defended the agreement as essential for India’s energy security and economic growth, insisting it would not limit the country’s nuclear weapons program or foreign policy independence.

The parliamentary victory gives Singh new political momentum, but the controversy surrounding the agreement underscored the deep divisions in India over closer strategic ties with the United States.

# India’s Government Survives No-Confidence Vote Over Landmark Nuclear Deal With United States

**New Delhi** — India’s coalition government survived a dramatic no-confidence vote in Parliament after a fierce political battle over a landmark civilian nuclear cooperation agreement with the United States, preserving Prime Minister Manmohan Singh’s administration and clearing a critical domestic hurdle for one of the most consequential shifts in India’s foreign policy since the Cold War.

The vote, held in the Lok Sabha, India’s lower house of Parliament, followed the withdrawal of support by left-wing parties that had propped up Singh’s United Progressive Alliance government from outside since 2004. The Communist parties and their allies accused the government of compromising India’s strategic autonomy by moving ahead with the nuclear accord, arguing that the agreement would bind New Delhi too closely to Washington.

Despite the loss of leftist support, the government survived with the backing of new allies, most notably the Samajwadi Party, a regional party based in Uttar Pradesh. The final tally gave the government a narrow but decisive victory, allowing Singh to continue in office and proceed with implementation of the nuclear deal.

## A Vote That Became a Referendum on India’s Global Alignment

Although formally a confidence motion, the parliamentary showdown was widely seen as a referendum on the Indo-U.S. civil nuclear agreement. The deal, first announced in 2005 by Singh and U.S. President George W. Bush, aimed to end India’s decades-long nuclear isolation and permit international nuclear commerce with New Delhi, despite India’s status outside the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

Under the agreement, India would separate its civilian and military nuclear facilities and place civilian reactors under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards. In return, the United States and other countries would be able to sell nuclear fuel, technology and reactors to India for civilian energy production.

For Singh, the deal represented a historic opening. India’s growing economy faced severe energy shortages, and the government argued that access to global nuclear markets would help diversify energy supplies, reduce dependence on fossil fuels and support long-term development. Strategically, the agreement also symbolized a major transformation in India-U.S. relations, bringing the world’s largest democracy and the world’s most powerful country into closer alignment after decades of mistrust.

But opponents saw it differently.

## Left Parties Withdraw Support

The immediate trigger for the crisis was the government’s decision to move forward with talks at the International Atomic Energy Agency, a required step before seeking approval from the Nuclear Suppliers Group, the international cartel that regulates nuclear trade.

Left parties, including the Communist Party of India and the Communist Party of India-Marxist, warned that the agreement would undermine India’s independent foreign policy. They objected particularly to provisions in U.S. domestic legislation, including the Hyde Act, which they argued could expose India to American pressure on issues such as Iran, nuclear testing and defense policy.

The left had supported Singh’s coalition from outside Parliament, giving the government a working majority without joining the cabinet. Once they withdrew, the government was forced to prove that it still commanded the confidence of the Lok Sabha.

The opposition Bharatiya Janata Party also opposed the agreement, though for different reasons. The BJP, which had overseen India’s 1998 nuclear tests while in power, argued that the deal placed unacceptable restrictions on India’s nuclear sovereignty and could constrain future weapons development or nuclear testing.

This created an unusual alignment: left-wing parties suspicious of U.S. imperial influence and the Hindu nationalist BJP, normally ideological adversaries, both opposed the government on the nuclear deal.

## Samajwadi Party Emerges as Kingmaker

Singh’s survival depended on finding new support quickly. The key came from the Samajwadi Party, led by Mulayam Singh Yadav and Amar Singh, which reversed its earlier skepticism and announced support for the government after consultations with former President A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, a respected scientist associated with India’s nuclear and missile programs.

The Samajwadi Party’s backing changed the arithmetic in Parliament. It helped offset the withdrawal of left support and allowed the Congress-led coalition to assemble enough votes from smaller parties and independents.

The shift also reflected India’s highly fluid coalition politics. Regional parties often hold decisive influence in national governments, and their decisions may be shaped by a mixture of ideological positioning, state-level rivalries, electoral calculations and negotiations over policy or political influence.

## Parliamentary Drama and Allegations of Corruption

The debate before the vote was intense and at times chaotic. Singh defended the deal as essential for India’s future, insisting that it would not compromise national sovereignty. He argued that the agreement recognized India as a responsible nuclear power and would give the country access to technology and fuel long denied to it.

Opposition leaders accused the government of selling out India’s strategic independence and using improper means to secure votes. The session was overshadowed by sensational allegations of bribery when opposition lawmakers displayed bundles of cash in Parliament, claiming they had been offered money to abstain or support the government. The government denied wrongdoing, but the episode deepened public cynicism about coalition bargaining and parliamentary ethics.

Even so, the political outcome was clear: Singh’s government survived.

## Why the Nuclear Deal Mattered

The nuclear agreement was significant for several reasons.

First, it effectively ended India’s pariah status in the global nuclear order. Since India conducted its first nuclear test in 1974, it had faced restrictions on nuclear trade. Because India never signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, it had been excluded from many forms of international nuclear cooperation.

Second, the deal marked a strategic breakthrough with the United States. During the Cold War, India was officially non-aligned but maintained close defense and diplomatic ties with the Soviet Union, while the United States often tilted toward Pakistan. The nuclear accord signaled a new era in which Washington increasingly viewed India as a major Asian power and potential strategic partner.

Third, the agreement carried implications for the balance of power in Asia. Although neither government described the deal as anti-China, many analysts saw closer India-U.S. ties as part of a broader adjustment to China’s rise.

Fourth, the agreement strengthened India’s claim to exceptional status in the nuclear order. Unlike other countries outside the NPT, India was being offered access to nuclear commerce without giving up its nuclear weapons program. Supporters argued that India’s non-proliferation record justified the exception; critics said it weakened global non-proliferation norms.

## Domestic Politics: Singh’s Gamble

For Manmohan Singh, the no-confidence vote was a defining moment. Often described as a cautious technocrat rather than a mass politician, Singh took a major political risk by insisting on the nuclear deal despite opposition from former allies.

The Congress party leadership, including Sonia Gandhi, ultimately backed him. The decision showed that the government considered the nuclear agreement not merely a foreign policy initiative but a legacy-defining achievement.

By surviving the vote, Singh gained political momentum and demonstrated that he could stand firm on a major strategic issue. The victory also allowed his government to proceed with the remaining international steps required to operationalize the agreement.

## International Response

The United States welcomed the government’s survival, seeing it as essential for completing the agreement before the end of President Bush’s term. Washington had invested significant diplomatic capital in the deal, which required changes to U.S. law and approval by Congress.

After the confidence vote, India moved forward with an safeguards agreement at the International Atomic Energy Agency. The next crucial step was securing a waiver from the Nuclear Suppliers Group, which would allow member states to engage in civilian nuclear trade with India. That waiver was eventually granted, paving the way for final U.S. congressional approval of the agreement.

Other major powers, including France and Russia, also stood to benefit commercially from the opening of India’s nuclear energy market. Both countries later pursued nuclear cooperation with India.

## Criticism and Long-Term Questions

Despite the government’s victory, criticism of the nuclear deal did not disappear. Skeptics argued that the agreement’s energy benefits had been overstated, given the high cost and complexity of nuclear power projects. Others maintained that India had moved too close to the United States and risked limiting its diplomatic flexibility.

There were also continuing debates about whether the deal would affect India’s ability to conduct future nuclear tests. The Indian government insisted that India retained the sovereign right to test if necessary, while critics warned that testing could trigger the termination of cooperation and fuel supplies.

In practice, the deal’s long-term impact has been mixed. It transformed India’s international nuclear status and deepened strategic relations with the United States, but the expansion of nuclear power in India has been slower than some early projections suggested. Liability concerns, regulatory issues, costs and local opposition have complicated reactor projects.

Still, as a diplomatic achievement, the agreement marked a major turning point.

## A Turning Point in Indian Foreign Policy

The survival of Singh’s government was about more than parliamentary arithmetic. It confirmed a broader shift in India’s international posture: from Cold War-era suspicion of alignment with Washington toward a more pragmatic, interest-based partnership with the United States.

The vote also illustrated the tension at the heart of Indian foreign policy. India seeks access to advanced technology, global markets and strategic partnerships, but it remains deeply protective of sovereignty and independence. The nuclear deal forced Parliament to confront that balance directly.

By winning the confidence vote, Singh secured the political mandate he needed to complete the agreement. In doing so, his government survived one of the most serious crises of its tenure and pushed India into a new phase of global engagement.

The no-confidence vote thus became a defining episode in modern Indian politics: a moment when domestic coalition maneuvering, nuclear diplomacy and the future of India’s strategic identity converged on the floor of Parliament.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — President George W. Bush urged India to move quickly to finalize a landmark civilian nuclear cooperation agreement after Prime Minister Manmohan Singh narrowly survived a confidence vote in Parliament, a crucial political hurdle for the deal.

The vote, held Tuesday in New Delhi, allowed Singh’s government to continue pursuing the U.S.-India civil nuclear agreement, which would open India’s civilian nuclear sector to international commerce after decades of isolation.

The Bush administration welcomed the outcome, calling the agreement a historic step in U.S.-India relations and a key part of efforts to bring India closer to the global nonproliferation framework.

“This is an important day for India and for the U.S.-India partnership,” Bush said, according to administration officials. He urged Indian leaders to “move forward” so the agreement could be completed before the end of his presidency.

The deal would allow the United States to sell civilian nuclear fuel and technology to India, despite India not being a signatory to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. In return, New Delhi has agreed to separate its civilian and military nuclear programs and place civilian facilities under international inspection.

Singh had staked his government’s survival on the agreement, arguing that it is essential for India’s growing energy needs and its emergence as a global power. Critics in India, including communist parties that withdrew support from his coalition, argued the deal could compromise India’s strategic independence and draw the country too closely into Washington’s orbit.

With the confidence vote behind him, Singh must still secure approval from the International Atomic Energy Agency and the Nuclear Suppliers Group before the agreement can return to the U.S. Congress for final consideration.

U.S. officials have said time is short, with the Bush administration eager to complete the pact before leaving office in January. Supporters say the deal represents one of the most significant foreign policy achievements of Bush’s second term and a major turning point in relations between the world’s two largest democracies.

Opponents, however, have warned that making an exception for India could weaken global nonproliferation efforts.

For Singh, the vote was both a political rescue and a diplomatic opening. For Bush, it renewed hopes that a signature agreement with India could still be completed before his term ends.
